why.correct: Food passes through every part of the alimentary canal but never through an accessory organ. The pancreas sits outside the tube and sends its enzymes into it through a duct.
options: Correct. The pancreas makes digestive secretions and delivers them into the tube, but food never enters it.
Food passes through the esophagus on its way from the pharynx to the stomach, so it is part of the canal.
The pharynx is shared by food and air, and swallowed food passes through it, so it is part of the canal.
The large intestine is the last stretch of the tube, ending at the anus.

why.correct: Mechanical digestion makes pieces smaller and mixes them without breaking chemical bonds: chewing, churning and segmentation. Enzymes splitting molecules is chemical digestion, and glucose crossing the lining is absorption.
options: Correct. Grinding breaks the peanut into smaller pieces without changing its molecules.
Splitting starch breaks chemical bonds by hydrolysis, so this is chemical digestion.
Correct. Churning breaks up and mixes food physically.
Correct. This is segmentation, a mixing movement of the wall.
Moving a nutrient across the lining into the blood is absorption, not digestion.
Breaking peptide bonds is chemical digestion, done by enzymes.

why.correct: The mucosa comes first: the epithelium, then the lamina propria beneath it (with the thin muscularis mucosae at its base). Next is the submucosa, then the muscularis externa with its inner circular and outer longitudinal layers, and finally the serosa.
The submucosa is the connective tissue layer just outside the mucosa. It carries the larger blood vessels and lymphatic vessels and the submucosal plexus.
options: Correct. It lies between the mucosa and the muscle layers.
The mucosa is the innermost layer, lining the lumen.
The muscularis lies outside the submucosa, as circular and longitudinal muscle.
The serosa is the thin outer covering.

why.correct: The myenteric plexus lies between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers and controls motility.
options: Correct. Its position between the two muscle layers gives it control of their contractions.
The submucosal plexus lies in the submucosa, closer to the lumen, and controls secretion and local blood flow.
The vagus nerve reaches the gut from outside and synapses on enteric neurons; it is not a network within the wall.
The celiac ganglion is a sympathetic ganglion in front of the aorta, outside the gut wall.

why.correct: Ahead of the food, inhibitory enteric neurons release nitric oxide, which relaxes the circular muscle and widens the tube. If the muscle ahead contracted too, the food would be squeezed from both sides and could not move.
options: This step is right. Distension of the wall is the stimulus that starts the reflex.
This step is right. Stretch-sensitive enteric sensory neurons start the short reflex.
This step is right. Excitatory motor neurons release acetylcholine behind the food.
This is the error. The muscle ahead relaxes; the narrowing behind and widening ahead together push the food forward.
This step is right. The new stretch repeats the reflex, so the wave travels along the tube.

why.correct: This is segmentation. Alternating rings of contraction chop and remix the contents and press them against the lining, but they produce little net movement.
options: Fast forward movement needs a traveling contraction, which is peristalsis. The question says no wave travels.
Pushing contents backward would need a contraction wave traveling the other way. Rings that contract in place move contents both ways about equally.
Segmentation is itself a mixing movement, so the contents are being mixed.
Correct. Segmentation mixes contents with secretions and keeps them in contact with the absorptive lining without moving them far.

why.correct: Peristalsis needs relaxation ahead of the contents, and that relaxation comes from enteric inhibitory neurons releasing nitric oxide. Without them the smooth muscle stays contracted, the segment stays narrow, and no wave can pass through it. The normal intestine above it fills and swells. This condition is called Hirschsprung disease.
options: The segment is narrow and contracted, not floppy. Smooth muscle has its own tone; what the missing neurons remove is the signal that relaxes it.
The problem is movement, not absorption. The block is in the muscle wall, and stool never reaches the segment's lining in quantity.
Sympathetic fibers tighten sphincters rather than open them, and the biopsy showed missing enteric neurons, not missing sympathetic fibers.
Correct. Without inhibitory enteric neurons, the muscle cannot relax, so the segment acts as a fixed narrowing.

why.correct: The sympathetic division turns the enteric nervous system down and tightens the sphincters, so movement and secretion fall and contents are held in place. Its arterioles narrow, shifting blood toward working muscle.

variables.name: Motility (strength and frequency of contractions)
variables.why: Sympathetic fibers inhibit enteric neurons, so fewer slow waves reach threshold and contractions weaken.

variables.name: Secretion by glands in the gut wall
variables.why: Sympathetic activity inhibits the submucosal plexus neurons that drive secretion.

variables.name: Tone of the gut sphincters
variables.why: Norepinephrine acts on alpha-1 receptor proteins on sphincter smooth muscle and contracts it.

variables.name: Blood flow to the gut
variables.why: Sympathetic vasomotor fibers constrict the gut's arterioles through alpha-1 receptor proteins.

why.correct: Acid releases secretin and fat releases CCK. Secretin brings in bicarbonate to neutralize the acid; CCK brings in bile and pancreatic enzymes to digest the fat. Both hold back the stomach, so the intestine receives new material only as fast as it can process it.

variables.name: Secretin in the blood
variables.why: Acid arriving in the first part of the small intestine releases secretin.

variables.name: Cholecystokinin (CCK) in the blood
variables.why: Fats and protein fragments in the first part of the small intestine release CCK.

variables.name: Bicarbonate-rich fluid from the pancreas
variables.why: Secretin acts on the pancreas and the ducts that carry bile to release a watery bicarbonate-rich fluid.

variables.name: Contraction of the gallbladder
variables.why: CCK contracts the gallbladder's smooth muscle, pushing bile into the intestine.

variables.name: Rate of stomach emptying
variables.why: Both secretin and CCK slow stomach emptying, so less arrives until the intestine has handled what it has.

why.correct: A long reflex leaves the gut, is integrated in the central nervous system and returns through autonomic nerves. This vagus-to-brainstem-to-vagus loop is often called a vagovagal reflex.
options: Correct. The loop runs through the brainstem and returns in the vagus nerve, so it is a long reflex.
A short reflex stays entirely within the enteric nervous system in the gut wall. This one travels to the brainstem.
A somatic reflex acts on skeletal muscle. This reflex acts on glands through the autonomic nervous system.
The signal travels in nerves, not through a hormone in the blood.

why.correct: Acid in the first part of the small intestine releases secretin, which makes the pancreas and the ducts that carry bile secrete bicarbonate. Once the acid is neutralized, secretin release falls: a negative feedback loop.
options: Gastrin comes from the stomach and raises stomach acid secretion, which would add to the acid rather than neutralize it.
Motilin is released between meals and triggers housekeeping contractions; it does not control bicarbonate secretion.
Correct. Secretin is the hormone released by acid in the intestine, and its main target is the bicarbonate secretion of the pancreas.
The myenteric plexus controls muscle, not the pancreas, and stopping all contractions would not neutralize acid.

why.correct: The pancreas lies against the back wall of the abdomen, behind the peritoneum, which covers only its front surface.
options: The stomach is wrapped in visceral peritoneum and hangs from folds of it, the omenta.
Most of the small intestine hangs on a mesentery and is covered by visceral peritoneum.
The gallbladder sits on the underside of the liver, largely covered by peritoneum.
Correct. The pancreas sits behind the peritoneum, fixed to the back wall.

why.correct: The greater omentum hangs like an apron from the stomach's lower curve in front of the intestines. It is fatty and rich in immune cells and tends to stick to inflamed organs, which can contain an infection.
options: The lesser omentum is a smaller fold running from the stomach's upper curve to the liver. It does not drape over the intestines.
The parietal peritoneum lines the abdominal wall; it does not hang from the stomach.
Correct. Its apron-like position and fat content match the description.
The mesentery holds the small intestine to the back wall and carries its vessels. It does not hang from the stomach in front of the intestines.

why.correct: The pellet stretches the wall and triggers the peristaltic short reflex through the myenteric plexus, which is entirely within the wall. The intestine propels the pellet with no connection to the central nervous system.
options: The vagus nerve adjusts gut activity but does not start it. The enteric nervous system can run peristalsis with no outside input.
Correct. The ENS contains sensory neurons, interneurons and motor neurons, so the whole reflex can run inside the wall.
Sympathetic signals and epinephrine inhibit gut motility; they do not start peristalsis.
Gap junctions spread contraction locally, but enteric neurons shape it into a wave with relaxation ahead. The whole length does not contract at once.

why.correct: Motilin is released between meals, every 90 to 120 minutes, and triggers strong waves of contraction that sweep from the stomach through the small intestine. A drug that imitates it speeds stomach emptying.
options: This describes cholecystokinin, which also slows stomach emptying rather than speeding it.
This describes gastrin.
Correct. This is motilin's effect, so stimulating its receptor proteins strengthens stomach contractions.
This describes secretin, which also slows stomach emptying.

why.correct: The parietal peritoneum is the layer lining the inside of the abdominal wall.
options: Correct. It lines the body wall, just inside the muscles.
The visceral peritoneum covers the organs themselves.
The peritoneal cavity is the thin space between the two layers, not a layer.
The greater omentum is a fold hanging from the stomach, not the lining of the wall.

why.correct: Slow waves set the maximum rhythm but rarely trigger contraction alone. Acetylcholine from enteric and vagal neurons, and hormones such as gastrin, depolarize the muscle so each wave reaches threshold and fires action potentials. The rate stays about 3 per minute; what changes is whether each wave produces a contraction.
options: The question says the slow waves continue in those quiet stretches at their usual rate. The rhythm is not what changes.
Correct. Excitatory input decides whether a slow wave reaches threshold, and that is why contraction follows the meal while the rhythm stays the same.
The stomach wall is smooth muscle throughout; skeletal muscle is found only at the two ends of the tube.
Gap junctions do not open and close with meals in this way; the change is in how close the membrane is to threshold.

why.correct: The uvula is the small flap hanging from the middle of the back edge of the soft palate.
options: Correct. It hangs in the midline from the soft palate.
The soft palate is the muscular back part of the roof of the mouth; the uvula hangs from it.
The palatine tonsils sit to each side, between the two arches, not in the midline.
The lingual frenulum is under the tongue, on the floor of the mouth.

why.correct: Dentin forms the bulk of the tooth, under the enamel of the crown and the cementum of the root, around the pulp cavity.
options: Enamel is the thin, hard cap on the outside of the crown only.
Correct. Dentin is the thick layer that makes up most of the tooth.
Cementum is a thin layer on the outside of the root.
Pulp fills the central cavity and root canals, inside the dentin.

why.correct: The lower esophageal sphincter is the zone at the junction of the esophagus and the stomach, just below the diaphragm.
options: The upper esophageal sphincter is at the top of the esophagus, where it meets the pharynx.
Correct. It guards the junction with the stomach.
The diaphragm is the sheet of muscle the esophagus passes through; it helps the sphincter but is not the pinned structure.
The trachea lies in front of the esophagus in the neck and upper chest, not at the stomach.

why.correct: The 20 deciduous teeth are 8 incisors, 4 canines and 8 molars. Premolars appear only in the permanent set, replacing the deciduous molars.
options: Children have 8 deciduous incisors, the same number as adults.
Children have 4 deciduous canines.
Correct. The deciduous set has no premolars.
Children have 8 deciduous molars; the permanent molars then erupt behind them.

why.correct: Enamel has no living cells, so drilling it causes no sensation. Dentin, just beneath it, is crossed by tubules holding extensions of living cells, and disturbing them causes pain, before the drill is anywhere near the pulp.
options: Cementum covers the root, below the gum, not the crown under the enamel.
The periodontal ligament lies outside the root, attaching it to the socket. A drill in the crown does not reach it.
Reaching the pulp would mean drilling through all the dentin first. Pain starts earlier, in the dentin.
Correct. Dentin lies directly under the enamel and is sensitive.

why.correct: The pharyngeal phase is the reflex that seals the airway: vocal fold closure, elevation of the larynx and tipping of the epiglottis, timed by the swallowing center in the medulla and pons. The patient can still start a swallow voluntarily, but the reflex that should protect the airway is slow or weak, so liquid enters the larynx.
options: He can chew and push food back, so the voluntary phase works.
Correct. Airway protection is part of the pharyngeal phase, and its center is in the damaged brainstem.
The esophageal phase starts only after the bolus has passed the pharynx. Liquid entering the larynx means the failure is earlier.
Thin liquids need no lubrication. Their danger is that they move fast and reach the larynx before a weak reflex closes it.

why.correct: The voluntary phase delivers the bolus to the oropharynx, which triggers the brainstem reflex. The airway is sealed first (vocal folds closing at the very start), then the larynx rises under the epiglottis and the upper sphincter opens. Peristalsis then carries the bolus through the esophagus to the relaxed lower sphincter.
Breathing stops for about a second during the pharyngeal phase. The airway is closed, so air cannot move, and a breath in at that moment would pull food into the larynx.
options: This step is right. The soft palate lifts and keeps food out of the nose.
This step is right. Closing the vocal folds seals the airway from inside, at the very start of the swallow.
This step is right. The larynx tucks under the tongue and the epiglottis covers it.
This is the error. Breathing pauses during the pharyngeal phase.
This step is right. The constrictors contract from top to bottom as the upper esophageal sphincter opens.

why.correct: Atropine removes the parasympathetic drive to the salivary glands, so the mouth becomes dry. Less saliva means less amylase, a stickier bolus that is harder to swallow, and weaker taste.

variables.name: Volume of saliva
variables.why: Parasympathetic fibers drive the large, watery flow of saliva through muscarinic receptor proteins, and atropine blocks them.

variables.name: Starch digestion in the mouth
variables.why: Less saliva means less salivary amylase mixed with the food.

variables.name: Ease of swallowing dry food
variables.why: With little saliva and mucus, chewed food does not bind into a slippery bolus.

variables.name: Ability to taste a dry cracker
variables.why: Taste molecules must dissolve in saliva to reach the taste buds.

why.correct: The parotid glands sit in front of and below each ear, over the masseter. Mumps, a viral infection prevented by vaccination, typically swells them.
options: The submandibular glands lie under the body of the mandible, not in front of the ears.
The sublingual glands lie in the floor of the mouth under the tongue.
Correct. Their position in front of the ears matches the swelling.
The palatine tonsils sit inside the throat, between the arches at the back of the mouth, where swelling cannot be seen from outside.

why.correct: Amylase keeps working inside the swallowed bolus until stomach acid penetrates it and lowers the pH below the enzyme's working range, often after half an hour or more.
options: The enzyme travels inside the bolus, so it continues after swallowing.
Correct. Acid denatures amylase once it reaches the inside of the bolus.
A sphincter controls the passage of the whole bolus; it cannot separate an enzyme from food.
Bile enters the small intestine, after the stomach, and it does not break down enzymes.

why.correct: Lysozyme damages bacterial walls, IgA binds microbes on mucous membranes, bicarbonate buffers acids made by mouth bacteria, and mucus coats and protects the lining. Amylase digests starch, and bile is not in saliva.
options: Correct. Lysozyme attacks bacteria.
Correct. IgA is the antibody class secreted onto mucous membranes.
Correct. Bicarbonate buffers acid that would dissolve enamel.
Salivary amylase digests starch; it is not a defense.
Correct. Mucus coats the lining and traps microbes.
Bile is made by the liver and enters the small intestine. It is not part of saliva.

why.correct: The muscularis externa of the esophagus is skeletal muscle in its upper third, mixed in its middle and smooth in its lower third. Blocking skeletal neuromuscular junctions stops the upper part, while the smooth muscle below still contracts.
options: Correct. The upper third is skeletal muscle driven directly by brainstem motor neurons.
The lower third is smooth muscle, which the drug does not affect.
Only the skeletal part is affected, so the esophagus is not affected evenly.
The middle third is a mixture of skeletal and smooth muscle, so it is weakened, but the upper third, which is all skeletal, is the part that stops.

why.correct: This is heartburn from reflux. Lying down after a large meal lets acid flow back past the lower esophageal sphincter into the esophagus, whose squamous lining has few defenses against it. Frequent reflux like this is GERD.
options: Heart pain is usually brought on by exertion and is not relieved by antacids. Chest pain always needs heart causes ruled out, but this pattern fits reflux.
Correct. Timing with meals and lying down, and relief with antacids, point to acid reflux.
Food stuck at the top of the esophagus causes trouble swallowing and a feeling of something in the throat, not nightly burning after meals.
Parotid inflammation causes swelling in front of the ears, not pain behind the sternum.

why.correct: Enteric inhibitory neurons relax gut smooth muscle mainly with nitric oxide, helped by VIP. That is how parasympathetic activity relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter.
options: Correct. Nitric oxide from inhibitory neurons relaxes the sphincter's smooth muscle.
The lower esophageal sphincter is smooth muscle, and acetylcholine contracts gut smooth muscle rather than relaxing it.
Norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptor proteins tightens gut sphincters; it is the sympathetic effect.
The sphincter opens by relaxation of its muscle. It relaxes even when you swallow lying down or upside down.

why.correct: The esophagus is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, built for abrasion, not acid. The stomach's lining has its own defenses against acid, which the stomach topic explains. Where the two linings meet, the change is abrupt.
options: Acid damages the lining first; muscle thickness has nothing to do with why the lining is vulnerable.
Correct. The squamous lining lacks the acid defenses of the stomach's lining.
In the chest the esophagus has an adventitia, not a serosa, and neither layer absorbs acid.
The acid comes from the stomach, so it is diluted, not concentrated, when it refluxes.

why.correct: The lingual frenulum anchors the underside of the tongue to the floor of the mouth. When it is short (tongue-tie), it tethers the tip, which cannot move forward and is pulled into a notch.
options: The labial frenulum joins a lip to the gum. It does not tether the tongue.
The uvula hangs from the soft palate and does not attach to the tongue.
Correct. A short lingual frenulum is tongue-tie.
The soft palate is the back of the roof of the mouth; it does not hold the tongue tip.

why.correct: The lower esophageal barrier has two parts: the sphincter's smooth muscle and the diaphragm around it. A hiatal hernia removes the second part, so reflux and heartburn increase, while peristalsis above is unchanged.

variables.name: Pressure holding the lower esophageal sphincter closed
variables.why: The diaphragm's pinch normally adds to the sphincter's own smooth muscle; with the hernia that part is lost.

variables.name: Episodes of reflux into the esophagus
variables.why: A lower closing pressure lets stomach contents push back into the esophagus more easily.

variables.name: Heartburn
variables.why: More acid reaches the unprotected squamous lining of the esophagus.

variables.name: Time for a bolus to travel down the esophagus
variables.why: Peristalsis in the body of the esophagus is unaffected; only the barrier at the bottom is weakened.

why.correct: The fundus is the dome that bulges up beside the opening from the esophagus, under the diaphragm.
options: Correct. It rises above the level of the esophageal opening.
The cardia is the small region right around the esophageal opening, not the dome beside it.
The body is the large central region below the fundus.
The pyloric antrum is the wide part of the pyloric region, near the outlet.

why.correct: Parietal cells are the large, rounded cells that bulge from the upper part of the gland wall. They secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
options: Chief cells are smaller, granule-filled cells concentrated lower in the gland.
Correct. Their size, shape and position in the upper gland identify them.
Enteroendocrine cells are few and sit near the base of the gland.
Mucous neck cells line the neck of the gland, just below the pit, and are not the large bulging cells.

why.correct: Rugae are the large folds of mucosa and submucosa in an empty or partly filled stomach. They flatten as the stomach fills.
options: Correct. These are the visible folds of the lining.
Gastric pits are microscopic openings in the surface, too small to see as folds.
The oblique layer is muscle in the wall, not folds of the lining.
The lesser curvature is the short inner edge of the stomach.

why.correct: Carbonic anhydrase makes carbonic acid, which splits into H+ and bicarbonate. The proton pump moves H+ into the lumen against a huge gradient, Cl− follows through channels, and the two make hydrochloric acid outside the cell. Meanwhile the bicarbonate goes to the blood.

Blocking the final step of acid secretion raises the stomach's pH, so less pepsin is activated and less bicarbonate goes to the blood. The rise in pH also removes the negative feedback on gastrin, which rises.

variables.name: pH of the stomach contents
variables.why: With the pump blocked, far less H+ is moved into the lumen, so the contents are less acidic.

variables.name: Conversion of pepsinogen to pepsin
variables.why: Pepsinogen needs acid, below about pH 5, to cut itself into pepsin.

variables.name: Gastrin in the blood
variables.why: Low pH normally releases somatostatin, which shuts gastrin off. Without the acid, that brake is removed and G cells keep releasing gastrin.

variables.name: Bicarbonate added to the blood by the stomach (alkaline tide)
variables.why: One bicarbonate enters the blood for each H+ secreted, so less acid means less alkaline tide.

why.correct: Chief cells, mostly at the base of the gastric glands, make and store pepsinogen and release it into the gland's lumen.
options: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
Correct. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase.
G cells are enteroendocrine cells that release gastrin into the blood.
Surface mucous cells secrete mucus and bicarbonate.

why.correct: In acid, pepsinogen changes shape and removes a short piece of itself, uncovering its active site. The pepsin formed then activates more pepsinogen, a positive feedback loop.
options: Bicarbonate raises the pH, which would keep pepsinogen inactive; that is part of how the mucus layer protects the lining.
Intrinsic factor binds vitamin B12, not pepsinogen.
Gastrin is a hormone released into the blood; it stimulates acid secretion but does not cut pepsinogen.
Correct. Acid starts the activation, and pepsin then speeds it up.

why.correct: Pepsinogen is a zymogen: its active site is covered until acid outside the cell triggers its conversion to pepsin. Stored inside the cell, it cannot digest the cell's proteins.
options: Every cell is full of protein, including its membranes and enzymes.
Intrinsic factor is made by parietal cells and binds vitamin B12, not pepsinogen.
Correct. Being made and stored as an inactive zymogen protects the cell that makes it.
The mucus layer lies on the surface of the lining, outside the cells, not around granules inside them.

why.correct: Parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which binds B12 in the small intestine so the lining of its last part can absorb it. Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells removes intrinsic factor, so dietary B12 passes through unabsorbed. Injections bypass the gut. This is pernicious anemia.
options: Acid helps free B12 from food proteins; it does not destroy it. Her problem is the opposite: she has lost her parietal cells and has little acid.
Pepsin frees B12 from the proteins it is bound to in food; it does not inactivate the vitamin.
Her liver can store B12. The problem is getting B12 across the intestinal lining.
Correct. The problem is absorption, not intake, so more dietary B12 would not help.

why.correct: Prostaglandins made in the stomach lining increase mucus and bicarbonate secretion and blood flow to the mucosa. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen block prostaglandin production, so the mucosal barrier weakens and normal amounts of acid and pepsin can erode the lining.
options: Correct. Removing prostaglandins removes part of the mucosal barrier.
The question says her acid secretion is normal. NSAID ulcers come from a weaker barrier, not more acid.
NSAIDs can irritate the lining on contact, but their main effect is throughout the body, through blocked prostaglandin production. Ulcers form even when the drug is given by injection.
Pepsinogen is activated by acid in the lumen, outside the cells. Ibuprofen does not change that.

why.correct: The mucosal barrier includes alkaline mucus, tight junctions, rapid cell renewal, mucosal blood flow and prostaglandins that support the others. Pepsin works best in acid, and the stomach is lined by simple columnar epithelium.
options: Correct. The mucus holds bicarbonate, keeping the cell surface near pH 7.
Correct. Tight junctions stop acid leaking between the cells.
Correct. Rapid renewal replaces damaged surface cells quickly.
Correct. Prostaglandins increase mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow.
Pepsin works best near pH 2 and is inactive near neutral pH, which is why the alkaline surface protects the cells.
The stomach is lined by simple columnar epithelium. Stratified squamous epithelium lines the esophagus, which has little acid defense.

why.correct: A falling pH inhibits gastrin release: below about pH 3, D cells release somatostatin, which shuts the G cells off. This negative feedback limits acid secretion.
options: This step is right. Peptides and amino acids stimulate G cells directly.
This step is right. Gastrin is a hormone carried by the blood.
This step is right. Gastrin acts mainly through histamine-releasing cells and partly on parietal cells.
This step is right. Increased acid secretion lowers the pH of the contents.
This is the error. Low pH inhibits gastrin release through somatostatin.

why.correct: Sham feeding isolates the cephalic phase. Food acting on the head drives the vagus nerves, which stimulate acid and gastrin release without any food or stretch in the stomach.

variables.name: Vagal signals to the stomach
variables.why: The sight, smell, taste and chewing of food act on the hypothalamus and medulla oblongata, which increase vagal output.

variables.name: Acid secretion by the stomach
variables.why: Acetylcholine from vagal and enteric neurons stimulates the parietal cells: the cephalic phase.

variables.name: Gastrin in the blood
variables.why: Vagal signals stimulate the G cells to release gastrin even with no food in the stomach.

variables.name: Stretch of the stomach wall
variables.why: No food was swallowed, so the stomach does not fill.

why.correct: The cephalic phase is driven by the head: the smell, sight, taste or thought of food increases vagal output to the stomach before any food arrives.
options: Correct. The stimulus acts on the brain, and the vagus nerves carry the signal to the stomach.
The gastric phase needs food in the stomach, stretching it and stimulating the G cells.
The intestinal phase begins when chyme enters the small intestine, and it mostly inhibits secretion.
The esophageal phase is part of swallowing, not a phase of gastric secretion.

why.correct: The small intestine sets the pace of gastric emptying. Fat arriving there is the strongest stimulus for CCK release and the enterogastric reflex, which weaken the antrum's contractions and tighten the pylorus. Carbohydrate empties fastest.
options: Stretch of the stomach speeds emptying rather than slowing it, and equal meals stretch it similarly.
Gastrin is released by protein and stretch, not mainly by fat, and its effect is on acid secretion.
Correct. Signals from the intestine, not from the stomach, hold a fatty meal back.
The stomach absorbs almost no nutrients; rice leaves faster because carbohydrate triggers weaker braking signals from the intestine.

why.correct: As the sphincter closes, only a small squirt of liquid chyme gets through. The rest is forced back into the body of the stomach, and the collision grinds and mixes it. Repeated waves turn food into chyme.
options: Emptying happens a few milliliters per wave, over hours, not all at once.
Correct. This backward throw is how the stomach grinds food into particles small enough to pass.
The closure is part of mixing, not a pause in it.
The contents are thrown back into the body of the stomach. The lower esophageal sphincter stays closed.

why.correct: Vomit carries H+ and Cl− from the stomach. For each H+ the parietal cells secrete, a bicarbonate ion enters the blood, and when that acid is lost instead of reaching the intestine, the bicarbonate stays. The blood becomes alkaline. Potassium is lost too, so hypokalemia is common.
options: Bicarbonate-rich fluid is secreted further down the intestine. Vomiting mainly loses acid from the stomach.
Potassium falls with repeated vomiting: it is lost in the vomit and, even more, in the urine.
The kidneys respond over hours to days and cannot fully correct the change while acid keeps being lost, especially with water loss.
Correct. Losing stomach acid leaves extra bicarbonate in the blood.

why.correct: During vomiting the stomach and lower esophageal sphincter relax. The diaphragm and abdominal wall muscles contract together, raising the pressure around the stomach and driving its contents up and out.
options: The stomach is relaxed during the expulsion. Its wall is the container, not the pump.
The esophagus is a passive route during expulsion; it does not pump contents upward.
Correct. Skeletal muscles of breathing and the abdominal wall provide the force.
A sphincter controls an opening; it cannot push the whole stomach's contents.

why.correct: The three stimuli amplify each other, so removing one cuts the combined effect by much more than a third. And much of gastrin's effect passes through the histamine-releasing cells, so blocking histamine also blunts gastrin.
options: Parietal cells respond to acetylcholine and gastrin as well; that is why a proton pump inhibitor, which blocks the final step, is even stronger.
H2 blockers act on H2 receptor proteins. The pump is blocked by a different drug class, proton pump inhibitors.
Somatostatin is released by low pH. An H2 blocker raises the pH, if anything reducing somatostatin.
Correct. Mutual amplification, and gastrin's reliance on histamine, make histamine a strong lever.

why.correct: H. pylori swims into the mucus layer, where the pH is near neutral, and its enzyme urease makes a base that buffers the acid in its surroundings. The infection inflames the lining and weakens the mucosal barrier.
options: It lives on and in the mucus over the surface cells, not inside parietal cells.
H. pylori does not rely on spores in the stomach; it survives as an active spiral bacterium.
Many infected people secrete normal or even increased amounts of acid.
Correct. The mucus niche and the base made by its urease protect it.

why.correct: The jejunum is the middle region, coiled mostly in the upper left abdomen, between the duodenum and the ileum.
options: The duodenum is the short, curved first part near the stomach.
Correct. It follows the duodenum and lies mostly in the upper left.
The ileum is the last region, coiled lower down on the right and in the pelvis.
The large intestine frames the small intestine around the edges.

why.correct: The duodenum is the short, curved first region of the small intestine, which receives chyme from the stomach.
options: The jejunum follows the duodenum and is much longer and coiled.
The ileum is the final region, low on the right.
Correct. It is the first, short, C-shaped region.
The pyloric antrum is part of the stomach, just before the pylorus.

why.correct: The ileum is the only place where vitamin B12, bound to intrinsic factor, is absorbed. Without it, B12 from food cannot be taken up, so it must be given by injection.
options: Lactase sits in the brush border of the whole small intestine and is most active in the jejunum, which remains.
Stomach acid is made by the stomach, which is untouched.
Correct. Removing the ileum removes the site of B12 absorption.
Insulin comes from the pancreatic islets, not the intestine.

why.correct: Peyer's patches, clusters of lymphoid nodules in the wall, are most numerous in the ileum, the stretch closest to the bacteria-rich large intestine.
options: Correct. They cluster in the ileum.
The duodenum has few Peyer's patches; its distinctive feature is the duodenal glands.
The jejunum has few; it is recognized by its tall circular folds and villi.
They are concentrated in the ileum, not spread evenly.

why.correct: Chyme leaves the stomach at a pH near 2 and hits the first part of the duodenum before the pancreas's bicarbonate has mixed in. The alkaline mucus of the duodenal glands coats and protects that lining. That is also where most small-intestine ulcers form.
options: Most fat is absorbed further along, mainly in the jejunum, and alkaline mucus does not absorb fat.
The migrating motor complex starts in the stomach and is driven by motilin; it has nothing to do with mucus secretion.
Correct. The alkaline mucus meets the incoming acid.
Vitamin B12 is absorbed at the far end of the small intestine, in the ileum.

why.correct: Normal: 3 × 10 × 20 = 600 times a smooth tube. With flat villi: 3 × 1 × 20 = 60. That is one tenth of normal, so absorption falls roughly tenfold.
options: Losing a factor of 10 cuts the surface far more than in half.
Correct. 60 is one tenth of 600.
A twentyfold loss would mean losing the microvilli, which remain here.
The microvilli stand on the villi, so flattening the villi removes most of the surface they sit on.

why.correct: Circular folds are ridges up to about 1 cm tall, each covered in villi 0.5 to 1 mm tall. Each villus is covered in absorptive cells, and each cell carries a few thousand microvilli about 1 µm tall.

Lactase, sucrase, maltase and the peptidases are brush border enzymes, anchored in the membrane of the microvilli. Pepsin comes from the stomach's chief cells, and salivary amylase from the salivary glands.
options: Correct. Lactase splits lactose at the brush border.
Correct. Sucrase splits sucrose at the brush border.
Pepsin is secreted by chief cells in the stomach and stops working at the higher pH of the small intestine.
Correct. Maltase splits maltose into two glucose.
Salivary amylase is made in the salivary glands and works in the mouth and inside the swallowed bolus.
Correct. Peptidases split short peptides into amino acids.

why.correct: Lactase, built into the microvillus membrane, splits lactose into glucose and galactose right beside the transporters that absorb them.
options: Pepsin digests protein, not sugars.
Intestinal juice is mostly water and mucus with very little enzyme; lactose is split at the brush border.
Disaccharides such as lactose are not absorbed whole; they must be split into single sugars first.
Correct. Lactase is a brush border enzyme.

why.correct: Eating switches the small intestine from the fasting sweep of the migrating motor complex to the mixing pattern of segmentation. At the same time, the gastroileal reflex empties the ileum into the large intestine, making room for the new meal.

variables.name: Migrating motor complexes in the small intestine
variables.why: Eating stops the fasting pattern at once, and motilin release falls.

variables.name: Segmentation in the small intestine
variables.why: Chyme stretching the wall drives the enteric nervous system into the mixing pattern that follows a meal.

variables.name: Motility of the ileum
variables.why: Through the gastroileal reflex, food entering the stomach increases ileal contractions.

variables.name: Opening of the ileocecal sphincter
variables.why: The gastroileal reflex relaxes the sphincter, so leftover contents move into the large intestine.

why.correct: Absorptive cells package digested fat into droplets that are too large to cross into blood capillaries. They enter the lacteal in the core of each villus, and the fat-laden lymph looks milky.
options: Proteins are split into amino acids and absorbed into the blood capillaries, not the lymph.
The milky color comes from fat droplets, not from cells.
Intestinal juice is secreted into the lumen, not into the lymph.
Correct. Fat droplets in the lymph give it the milky look that named the lacteals.

why.correct: The intestinal glands normally secrete intestinal juice by moving chloride into the lumen, with sodium and water following. Locked-open channels drive this secretion far beyond normal, and the villi cannot take all that water back, so it leaves as watery stool.
options: Correct. The glands' secretion of chloride, sodium and water outpaces absorption.
Cholera leaves the villi intact; that is why a glucose and salt drink still works, since their absorptive cells still take up sodium with glucose.
The channels move chloride out of the cells into the lumen. Water follows the solute into the lumen, not out of it.
Cholera toxin acts on the chloride channels of the glands, not on the lymphatic vessels.

why.correct: Stem cells at the base of the intestinal glands divide all the time, and their daughters live only 3 to 5 days before being shed from the villus tips. A drug that stops cell division halts the supply, so within days the lining thins and breaks down.
options: The effect comes from blocked cell division throughout the body, not from delivery in bile.
Correct. Rapid renewal makes the lining one of the tissues most sensitive to drugs that kill dividing cells.
Villi are covered by epithelium over a core of connective tissue; only a few smooth muscle strands run in them, and smooth muscle is not what is damaged.
Chemotherapy does not digest enzymes. The enzymes disappear because the cells that carry them are not replaced.

why.correct: Both are folds of the mucosa and submucosa, but circular folds are permanent ridges that increase absorptive surface and slow the chyme, while rugae are temporary folds that let the stomach expand.
options: It is the other way round: rugae flatten, circular folds stay.
Both are folds of mucosa and submucosa; neither is a fold of muscle or serosa.
Both can be seen by eye; circular folds are up to about 1 cm tall.
Correct. Their permanence fits their job of adding absorptive area.

why.correct: This is the migrating motor complex. Released between meals, motilin triggers it, and it sweeps undigested particles, shed cells and bacteria toward the large intestine. Eating stops it.
options: Mixing with secretions is segmentation, which happens after meals. Secretin releases bicarbonate and does not start this pattern.
Correct. The migrating motor complex is the fasting housekeeper.
CCK contracts the gallbladder after fatty meals, not in fasting.
Relaxing the ileocecal sphincter after a meal is the gastroileal reflex.

why.correct: Brush border enzymes are part of the absorptive cells on the villi, so flattened villi carry far less of them. Lactase is the least abundant, so it is usually the first to fall short, and lactose goes undigested. Starch is still split to maltose by pancreatic enzymes, and the remaining maltase activity copes.
options: Celiac disease damages the intestinal lining, not the pancreas, and a pancreatic problem would affect rice starch too.
Pepsin digests protein, and the stomach is not affected by celiac disease.
Correct. Lactase falls first when villi are damaged.
If she could not digest starch, rice would cause symptoms too. Maltase is more abundant than lactase and is not the first to run short.

why.correct: Glucose, like amino acids, enters the blood capillaries of the villus and travels in the hepatic portal vein to the liver. The lacteal carries absorbed fat.
options: This step is right. Pancreatic enzymes leave maltose and short sugar chains.
This step is right. Mixing keeps fresh contents in contact with the brush border.
This step is right. Maltase is a brush border enzyme.
This is the error. Glucose enters the blood capillaries, not the lacteal.
This step is right. The hepatic portal vein carries absorbed sugars to the liver first.

why.correct: The jejunum has a thicker, redder wall, from its rich blood supply, and the tallest, most closely packed circular folds. The ileum is thinner and paler with low, sparse folds.
options: Correct. Thick red wall and tall folds mark the jejunum.
The ileum has a thinner, paler wall and low, sparse circular folds.
The duodenum is mostly retroperitoneal and fixed behind the peritoneum; a free loop is jejunum or ileum.
The large intestine is wider and does not have circular folds like these.

why.correct: The channels running between the plates of hepatocytes, from the edge of the lobule to the central vein, are the hepatic sinusoids: wide, leaky capillaries where portal and arterial blood mix.
options: Bile canaliculi are tiny grooves between neighboring hepatocytes, far too small to show as channels here, and they carry bile, not blood.
Correct. These are the hepatic sinusoids.
There is one central vein per lobule, running up its middle. The pinned channels run between the plates toward it.
Portal venules are the blue vessels at the corners of the lobule, in the portal triads. They feed the sinusoids.

why.correct: The green tube in the portal triad at the corner of the lobule is a bile duct. It collects bile from the bile canaliculi, which carry bile outward from the hepatocytes.
options: The portal arteriole is the red tube in the triad, a branch of the hepatic artery.
Hepatic veins are formed from central veins and leave the liver toward the inferior vena cava. They are not in the portal triads.
Correct. The third member of the portal triad is the bile duct.
Lymphatic vessels do run with the triads, but the pinned tube is drawn as the bile duct, and it carries bile out of the lobule.

why.correct: The cystic duct connects the gallbladder to the common hepatic duct. Bile flows through it both ways: into the gallbladder between meals and out after a meal.
options: The common hepatic duct is formed by the right and left hepatic ducts, before the gallbladder's duct joins it.
The common bile duct is the single tube below the point where the gallbladder's duct joins.
The right hepatic duct drains the right half of the liver. It does not reach the gallbladder.
Correct. The twisting duct leading from the gallbladder's neck is the cystic duct.

why.correct: The common bile duct forms where the cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct. It carries bile from both the liver and the gallbladder down to the duodenum.
options: Correct. This is the common bile duct.
The pancreatic duct runs the length of the pancreas and joins the common bile duct only at the duodenum.
The cystic duct is the short duct from the gallbladder, above the pinned duct.
The left hepatic duct drains the left half of the liver, high up inside the liver.

why.correct: Bile moves outward from the hepatocytes through canaliculi to the triad bile ducts, then through the hepatic ducts to the common hepatic duct. Between meals it backs up the cystic duct into the gallbladder, which concentrates it. After a meal, cholecystokinin contracts the gallbladder, and bile runs back down the cystic duct and the common bile duct to the ampulla and into the duodenum.

Blood from the intestine drains into the hepatic portal vein, whose branches in the portal triads empty into the sinusoids. Hepatocytes lining the sinusoids take up the drug before the blood reaches the central vein and the hepatic veins.
options: Correct. Portal vein branches feed the sinusoids, where blood bathes the hepatocyte plates.
The hepatic artery brings blood from the aorta, not from the intestine, and central veins collect blood after it has crossed the sinusoids.
Canaliculi and the bile duct carry bile out of the liver. Absorbed substances do not arrive through them.
Hepatic veins carry blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava; blood does not enter the liver that way.

why.correct: A blocked common bile duct stops bile from reaching the gut. Conjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood and urine, the feces lose their brown pigment, and less fat is digested and absorbed for lack of bile salts. Pancreatic juice still flows because its duct is below the blockage.

variables.name: Bile reaching the duodenum
variables.why: The only route for bile from both the liver and the gallbladder to the duodenum is through the common bile duct.

variables.name: Conjugated bilirubin in the blood
variables.why: Hepatocytes keep conjugating bilirubin, but bile cannot drain, so conjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood.

variables.name: Darkness of the urine
variables.why: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble, so the extra in the blood spills into the urine and darkens it.

variables.name: Brown color of the feces
variables.why: With no bilirubin reaching the intestine, bacteria make no stercobilin, so the feces turn pale.

variables.name: Fat in the feces
variables.why: Without bile salts, fat is not emulsified, so lipase has less surface to work on. Bile salts also carry the digested fat to the lining, so much of what is digested is not absorbed either.

variables.name: Pancreatic juice reaching the duodenum
variables.why: The stone sits above the junction with the pancreatic duct, so pancreatic juice still drains through the ampulla.

why.correct: Blocking the pancreatic duct stops the exocrine secretion reaching the gut: less lipase means fatty stools, and less bicarbonate leaves the duodenum more acidic. The islets are endocrine and release insulin straight into the blood, so insulin release is unchanged, and bile, with its own duct, still flows.

variables.name: Lipase reaching the duodenum
variables.why: Acinar cells still make lipase, but it cannot leave the gland through the blocked duct.

variables.name: Fat in the feces
variables.why: Pancreatic lipase does most fat digestion; bile can emulsify the fat, but without lipase it passes out undigested.

variables.name: pH of the chyme in the duodenum
variables.why: The bicarbonate from the duct cells no longer reaches the duodenum, so the stomach acid is neutralized less.

variables.name: Insulin released after the meal
variables.why: The islets release insulin into capillaries, not into the duct, so blocking the duct does not stop it (at least while the islets are undamaged).

variables.name: Bile reaching the duodenum
variables.why: The common bile duct is open, so bile still drains.

why.correct: Enteropeptidase is an enzyme fixed to the brush border of the duodenal lining. It makes the first trypsin, and trypsin activates the rest.
options: Correct. Enteropeptidase starts the cascade, and it exists only in the intestine.
Pepsin works in the stomach's acid and is inactivated when chyme is neutralized in the duodenum. It does not activate trypsinogen.
Cholecystokinin is a hormone that makes acinar cells release their enzymes. It does not cut trypsinogen.
Pancreatic amylase digests starch. It does not act on protein precursors.

why.correct: Bile salts have a hydrophobic face that sticks into fat and a hydrophilic face that stays in the water. They coat fat droplets and keep them small once churning breaks them up. Many small droplets have far more surface than a few large ones, and lipase works at that surface.
options: Bicarbonate neutralizes acid. It does not split the bonds in triglycerides; lipase does that.
Bilirubin is a waste pigment from old red blood cells, carried out in bile. It does not activate lipase.
Correct. Emulsification multiplies the surface area lipase can reach.
Cholesterol does not dissolve in water, and bile has to carry it with bile salts and phospholipids. It does not dissolve fat.

why.correct: The diameter falls 100-fold. Each small droplet has 1,000,000 times less volume, so there are 1,000,000 of them, and each has 10,000 times less area. 1,000,000 ÷ 10,000 = 100, so the total area rises 100-fold.
options: A 10-fold rise would come from a 10-fold fall in diameter. Here the diameter falls 100-fold.
Correct. Total surface rises by the same factor the diameter falls.
10,000 is how much smaller each droplet's own area is. It ignores that there are now a million droplets.
Volume is unchanged, but splitting fat into smaller droplets exposes more surface.

why.correct: About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the last part of the ileum and returned to the liver in the hepatic portal vein: the enterohepatic circulation. Without that segment they are lost in the feces. The liver makes new ones from cholesterol, but not fast enough, so too few bile salts reach the gut to emulsify a fatty meal.
options: Her gallbladder is normal and still concentrates bile. The problem is how much bile salt there is to concentrate.
Her pancreas is normal. Lipase is still released; it simply has too little emulsified fat surface to work on.
Correct. Loss of the terminal ileum breaks the enterohepatic circulation, so bile salts are lost in the feces.
Her liver is normal. Failure to conjugate bilirubin would cause jaundice, not fatty stools.

why.correct: Cholecystokinin relaxes the hepatopancreatic sphincter. If it contracted the sphincter, bile squeezed out of the gallbladder would have nowhere to go.
options: This step is right. Fat and protein in the duodenum trigger CCK release.
This step is right. CCK is a hormone and reaches its targets through the blood.
This step is right. Contraction empties the gallbladder.
This is the error. CCK relaxes the sphincter, opening the way into the duodenum.
This step is right. With the gallbladder contracting, the sphincter open and acinar cells stimulated, both fluids enter the duodenum.

why.correct: Acid lowers duodenal pH, which releases secretin. Secretin acts mainly on the duct cells, which pour out a large volume of bicarbonate-rich fluid. The bicarbonate neutralizes the acid, removing the stimulus: negative feedback.
options: Cholecystokinin is released by fat and protein, not acid, and it drives the enzyme-rich secretion of the acinar cells.
Correct. Acid releases secretin, which drives bicarbonate secretion.
The pancreas does respond: acid is the main stimulus for secretin, which drives bicarbonate secretion.
Trypsin is activated in the duodenum by enteropeptidase, never normally in the duct.

why.correct: This is acute pancreatitis. A gallstone stuck at the ampulla blocks the pancreatic duct. Enzymes are trapped, trypsin is activated inside the gland, and it activates the other enzymes, which digest pancreatic tissue. Lipase leaks from the damaged gland into the blood.
options: Bile salts emulsify fat; they do not digest tissue, and they do not cause pancreatitis by entering the blood.
A cystic duct stone causes gallbladder pain under the right ribs, and bile from the liver still reaches the duodenum. It does not block the pancreatic duct or raise lipase.
Stomach acid is neutralized in the duodenum and does not travel up the pancreatic duct.
Correct. Gallstones at the ampulla are one of the two commonest causes of acute pancreatitis.

why.correct: Hepatocytes make albumin and most clotting factors, store glucose as glycogen, and make bile salts from cholesterol. Insulin comes from the beta cells of the pancreatic islets, and lipase from the pancreatic acinar cells.
options: Correct. Albumin is the main plasma protein, and hepatocytes make it.
Correct. Hepatocytes make most clotting factors, using vitamin K for factors II, VII, IX and X.
Correct. Hepatocytes store glucose as glycogen after a meal and release it between meals.
Insulin is made by beta cells in the pancreatic islets, not by the liver.
Correct. Bile salts are made from cholesterol in hepatocytes.
Pancreatic lipase is made by acinar cells in the pancreas.

why.correct: Scar tissue squeezes the sinusoids, so portal vein pressure rises and fluid is pushed out of the congested abdominal vessels. At the same time, fewer working hepatocytes make less albumin, so the blood holds less water by osmosis and more fluid leaks into the tissues.
options: Correct. Portal hypertension and low albumin both push fluid out of the vessels.
Bilirubin causes jaundice. It is not the solute that holds water in the blood, and bile duct blockage is not the main problem in cirrhosis.
Poor fat absorption does not thin the blood or cause ascites.
Cirrhosis lowers clotting factor production, so bleeding, not clotting, is the usual problem.

why.correct: Blood enters at the portal triads, crosses the sinusoids and leaves by the central vein. Bile is secreted into canaliculi between hepatocytes and flows the other way, out to the bile ducts in the portal triads.
options: The central vein collects blood; it is where blood leaves, not where it enters, and bile never enters it.
Blood flows inward, but bile flows outward to the bile ducts.
Correct. The two flows run in opposite directions and never mix.
This reverses both flows.

why.correct: Between meals the hepatopancreatic sphincter stays closed. Bile secreted by the liver has nowhere to go but back up the common bile duct and into the gallbladder through the cystic duct.
options: The gallbladder's muscle contracts to empty it, not to fill it. Filling depends on the closed sphincter downstream.
Correct. A closed outlet diverts bile into the gallbladder.
Secretin raises bicarbonate secretion by duct cells; it does not close any duct.
Cholecystokinin is released after a meal and contracts the gallbladder; between meals it is low.

why.correct: The drug reaches the liver first in portal blood, and liver enzymes process it. Most becomes harmless, water-soluble products, but some becomes a reactive product. In an overdose so much reactive product forms that it kills hepatocytes. Detoxification can make a molecule more harmful as well as less.
options: The liver processes acetaminophen for excretion; storing it is not what causes damage.
Acetaminophen does not block blood vessels.
Correct. The liver's own processing creates the toxic product.
Acetaminophen does not act on bile salts.

why.correct: Acinar cells sit in grape-like clusters (acini) at the ends of the small ducts. They make the pancreatic enzymes and release them into the ducts.
options: Islet cells are the blue-green clusters with capillaries running through them. They release hormones into the blood, not enzymes into ducts.
Correct. The acini make the enzymes of pancreatic juice.
Duct cells line the ducts and add bicarbonate-rich fluid, not most of the enzymes.
Hepatocytes are liver cells, not pancreatic cells.

why.correct: Protein-digesting enzymes do not tell the gland's own proteins from food proteins. Kept as inactive precursors, they cannot digest the pancreas; they are switched on only in the duodenum, where enteropeptidase starts the cascade. When this fails, as in pancreatitis, the gland digests itself.
options: Correct. Zymogens protect the tissue that makes them.
Size is not the issue; activation cuts off a small piece and makes the enzyme slightly smaller, not larger.
Pancreatic juice never reaches the stomach, and the precursors do not digest protein anywhere.
Bile salts do not destroy trypsin or chymotrypsin; both work alongside bile in the duodenum.

why.correct: The cecum is the blind pouch at the start of the large intestine, in the lower right, below the ileocecal valve. The appendix hangs from it.
options: The ileum is the last part of the small intestine, which opens into the large intestine beside the pinned pouch.
The sigmoid colon is the S-shaped loop in the pelvis, at the other end of the colon.
Correct. The blind-ended pouch is the cecum.
The ascending colon starts above the cecum and rises up the right side.

why.correct: The sigmoid colon is the S-shaped loop in the pelvis between the descending colon and the rectum.
options: The descending colon runs straight down the left side, above the pinned loop.
Correct. The S-shaped loop is the sigmoid colon.
The rectum is the straighter segment that follows the loop, in front of the sacrum.
The transverse colon crosses the top of the abdomen.

why.correct: The teniae coli are ribbons of longitudinal smooth muscle running the length of the colon. There are three.
options: Epiploic appendages are the small fatty tags hanging from the surface, not the long ribbon.
Haustra are the pouches between the constrictions, which the teniae coli create.
A mesentery is a double sheet of peritoneum that suspends the gut from the body wall, not a muscle band on it.
Correct. The long ribbon of muscle is a tenia coli.

why.correct: Haustra are the pouches of the colon wall, formed because the shorter teniae coli bunch the wall up.
options: Correct. The rounded pouches are haustra.
Circular folds are ridges of the small intestine's mucosa and submucosa, seen from inside, not pouches of the whole wall.
Villi are microscopic projections of the small intestine's lining; the large intestine has none.
Rugae are folds in the lining of the stomach.

why.correct: Filling stretches the rectum. Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors signal the sacral cord, which sends parasympathetic output that contracts the rectum and relaxes the internal sphincter. The last gate, the external sphincter, is voluntary, so defecation happens only when you relax it.

The small intestine absorbs about 7 to 8 L a day. The colon absorbs most of what is left, about 1.3 of the 1.4 to 1.5 L that reaches it. The colon's share is large compared with what arrives, but small compared with the total.
options: The stomach absorbs very little water; its lining is built to hold acid in, not to absorb.
The colon absorbs about 90% of what reaches it, but only about 1.5 L arrives, a small fraction of the 9 L total.
Correct. Most absorption, of water as of nutrients, happens in the small intestine.
The rectum stores feces briefly and absorbs little.

why.correct: Sodium enters the epithelial cells through channels and is pumped out the other side by sodium–potassium pumps; chloride follows. With more solute on the blood side, water moves by osmosis. No transporter pumps water itself.
options: There is no water pump. Water moves passively, following the solute gradient that the sodium pumps set up.
Correct. Water follows the sodium the colon absorbs.
Bacteria do not ferry water into the wall.
Haustral contractions mix and press contents against the lining, which helps contact, but the pressure they make does not drive absorption.

why.correct: Slower movement gives the colon more time to absorb water, so stools become harder, drier and less frequent: opioid constipation. The cause is timing, not a change in the absorbing cells.

variables.name: Time feces spend in the colon
variables.why: Opioids depress the enteric neurons that drive haustral contractions and mass movements, so contents move more slowly.

variables.name: Water absorbed from each day's contents
variables.why: Contents stay longer in contact with the lining, so more sodium, and water with it, is absorbed.

variables.name: Water content of the stool
variables.why: More water absorbed leaves less in the feces.

variables.name: Number of stools per week
variables.why: Fewer mass movements deliver feces to the rectum less often, so the defecation reflex is triggered less often.

why.correct: A settled gut microbiota crowds out invaders by taking up space and nutrients. Broad-spectrum antibiotics kill many of these bacteria. A resistant species can then overgrow, and its toxins inflame the colon, causing diarrhea.
options: Correct. Loss of the normal flora's crowding-out effect lets the resistant species take over.
Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on the smooth muscle of the teniae coli.
Antibiotics do not block the colon's sodium channels. The toxins cause the diarrhea.
Pancreatic secretion is unaffected; missing enzymes would cause fatty stools, not a toxin-driven inflammatory diarrhea.

why.correct: Colon bacteria ferment fiber, change bilirubin into the brown pigment stercobilin, make some vitamins, and crowd out invaders. Bile salts come from the liver, and water is absorbed by the colon's own epithelial cells.
options: Correct. Saccharolytic fermentation makes acetate, propionate, butyrate and gas.
Correct. Bacteria turn bilirubin into urobilinogen and then stercobilin.
Correct. Some gut bacteria make vitamin K, though how much you absorb is uncertain.
Bile salts are made by hepatocytes. Bacteria only alter the few that escape reabsorption.
Correct. A settled community takes up space and nutrients that invaders would need.
Water absorption is done by the colon's epithelial cells, which absorb sodium and let water follow.

why.correct: The colon's outer longitudinal muscle is gathered into three ribbons, the teniae coli. They are shorter than the wall and keep up tone, so they bunch it into pouches.
options: Those fatty tags are the epiploic appendages. They hang from the colon but do not make the pouches.
The large intestine has no circular folds.
The large intestine has no villi.
Correct. The teniae coli gather the wall into haustra.

why.correct: The defecation reflex runs through the sacral cord, which is intact, so stretch still makes the rectum contract and the internal sphincter relax. The injury cuts the pathways to and from the brain, so he loses the sensation of urge and voluntary control of the external sphincter.
options: The reflex arc runs through the sacral cord, not the brain, so it works without signals from the brain.
Correct. The reflex survives; sensation and voluntary control are lost.
Sensation travels up through the injured cord, so he does not feel the urge normally, while the reflex contraction of the rectum still works.
The internal sphincter still relaxes by reflex, and voluntary control of the external sphincter needs signals from the brain, which the injury blocks.

why.correct: The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle, controlled by somatic motor neurons from the sacral cord. That is why you can control it voluntarily.
options: This statement is right. The internal sphincter is part of the muscularis externa.
This statement is right. Relaxing it is part of the defecation reflex.
This is the error. The external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control.
This statement is right. Tightening it holds feces in until the urge fades.
This statement is right. Closing the glottis and tightening the diaphragm and abdominal muscles raises abdominal pressure.

why.correct: Secreted chloride draws sodium and water into the lumen, so far more fluid than usual leaves the small intestine. The colon keeps absorbing, but it can take up only about 4 to 5 L a day. Everything above that leaves as diarrhea.
options: The colon is not destroyed. Cholera works mainly on the small intestine, and the colon keeps absorbing near its limit.
Cholera does not stop colon movement; the diarrhea comes from the volume of fluid.
Chloride does not block sodium channels; the colon's sodium absorption continues.
Correct. Secretory diarrhea overwhelms the colon's capacity.

why.correct: A solute that stays in the lumen holds water with it by osmosis, so more fluid reaches the colon than it can absorb. Bacteria fermenting the sorbitol add gas.
options: Secretory diarrhea comes from toxins that make cells secrete chloride. Sorbitol acts by staying in the lumen.
Correct. This is osmotic diarrhea.
Sorbitol does not damage the lining.
The defecation reflex is triggered by rectal stretch, not by sorbitol itself.

why.correct: Food stretching the stomach triggers the gastrocolic reflex, which increases colon motility and sets off mass movements. They push feces already in the colon into the rectum, and rectal stretch causes the urge.
options: Correct. The urge comes from contents already in the colon, moved by the reflex.
Breakfast itself takes a day or more to reach the rectum. What moves is yesterday's residue.
The external sphincter is voluntary; food does not relax it.
Cortisol does not drive colon contractions in this way.

why.correct: The large intestine's lining is flat, with no villi or circular folds, and goblet cells are far more common than in the small intestine. It is wider but much shorter.
options: The large intestine is about 1.5 m; the small intestine is several meters.
It is the other way round: villi are in the small intestine.
Teniae coli belong to the large intestine.
Correct. More goblet cells, no villi.

why.correct: The descending colon leads into the S-shaped sigmoid colon in the pelvis, which joins the rectum.
options: Correct. The sigmoid colon comes between the descending colon and the rectum.
The ileum is the end of the small intestine, before the cecum.
The appendix is a blind tube hanging from the cecum; contents do not pass through it.
The right colic flexure is the bend between the ascending and transverse colon, much earlier on the route.

why.correct: Diarrhea removes water, sodium, potassium and bicarbonate from the body. Blood volume falls, so the heart speeds up by reflex; potassium falls; and the loss of bicarbonate makes the blood more acidic.

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: Water and sodium lost in stool leave the extracellular fluid, including the plasma.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: The colon secretes potassium into the lumen, and large volumes of stool carry it out.

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: Intestinal fluid is rich in bicarbonate, which is lost with the stool.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Losing bicarbonate removes base from the blood's main buffer, so the blood becomes more acidic.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Lower blood volume lowers venous return and blood pressure, and the baroreceptor reflex raises sympathetic drive to the heart.

why.correct: Fiber is not digested by your enzymes. It holds water in the stool, feeds bacteria whose bodies add bulk, and makes a larger, softer mass. The stretch of a bigger mass triggers stronger contractions, so transit speeds up.
options: Your enzymes cannot digest most fiber; bacteria ferment some of it into short-chain fatty acids, not glucose for you.
Correct. Water held in bulky stool and stretch-driven contractions both help.
Fiber does not block sodium pumps; absorption continues normally.
Fiber feeds gut bacteria rather than killing them.

why.correct: Stomach acid kills many swallowed bacteria, and the small intestine moves its contents through in a few hours. In the colon contents stay a day or more, with little oxygen and plenty of undigested fiber, so bacteria multiply.
options: The colon does not secrete nutrients for bacteria; they live on undigested food, mostly fiber, and on mucus.
The colon has a thick mucus layer, which keeps bacteria off the lining.
Correct. Conditions, not special feeding, favor bacteria in the colon.
Bile salts are made in the liver, and they tend to hold bacteria down rather than feed them.

why.correct: The lacteal is the lymphatic capillary in the center of each villus. Chylomicrons are too large to enter blood capillaries, but they pass through the gaps between the lacteal's cells.
options: The blood capillary is the red loop around the lacteal. Sugars and amino acids enter it; chylomicrons are too large.
Correct. Chylomicrons enter the lacteal and travel in lymph.
The hepatic portal vein collects blood from the villus capillaries far downstream; it is not in the villus.
Central veins are in the liver lobules, not in the villi.

why.correct: Lactase, a brush border enzyme, splits lactose into glucose and galactose.
options: Sucrase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose.
Maltase splits maltose into two glucose.
Correct. Lactase splits lactose.
α-Dextrinase cuts the branch bonds of α-dextrins.

why.correct: Amylase in saliva, then from the pancreas, cuts starch into short pieces. Brush border enzymes finish them into glucose at the membrane. SGLT1 brings glucose in with sodium, a basolateral carrier lets it out, and the villus capillaries drain into the hepatic portal vein.

Pepsin starts, cutting inside chains. The pancreatic enzymes trypsin and chymotrypsin cut further inside the chains, and carboxypeptidase and aminopeptidase trim from the ends. Amino acids and small peptides enter the cells; the peptides are split inside, and amino acids leave into the blood.

Emulsification gives lipase more surface; lipase makes fatty acids and monoglycerides; micelles ferry them through the water next to the brush border; inside the cell they are rebuilt and packaged into chylomicrons, which are too large for blood capillaries and enter the lacteal instead.

Without enough lactase, lactose cannot be split or absorbed. It holds water in the small intestine by osmosis and is fermented by colon bacteria into gas and acids, giving bloating, hydrogen on the breath and osmotic diarrhea, while little of its sugar reaches the blood.

variables.name: Lactose reaching the colon
variables.why: Too little lactase is left at the brush border to split the lactose, so much of it passes through the small intestine intact.

variables.name: Water in the lumen of the small intestine
variables.why: Unabsorbed lactose is a solute that stays in the lumen and holds water there by osmosis.

variables.name: Hydrogen in the exhaled breath
variables.why: Colon bacteria ferment the lactose and make hydrogen; some is absorbed into the blood and breathed out.

variables.name: Water content of the stool
variables.why: The extra water, plus the solutes fermentation adds, is more than the colon can absorb, so the stool becomes loose.

variables.name: Rise in blood glucose after drinking
variables.why: Undigested lactose yields no glucose or galactose for SGLT1 to absorb, so blood glucose rises less than it would after the milk in a person with high lactase.

why.correct: Blocking lipase stops the splitting step, so triglycerides are neither taken into micelles nor absorbed. Fat and the vitamins that travel with it are lost in the feces, while carbohydrate digestion and absorption carry on unchanged.

variables.name: Monoglycerides formed in the lumen
variables.why: Lipase is the enzyme that splits triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides; blocking it leaves the triglycerides intact.

variables.name: Chylomicrons entering the lacteals
variables.why: Intact triglycerides cannot enter micelles or cross the brush border, so absorptive cells have less fat to package.

variables.name: Fat in the feces
variables.why: Undigested triglyceride passes through the gut and leaves in the stool.

variables.name: Absorption of vitamin D from the meal
variables.why: Vitamins that dissolve in fat are absorbed with micelles and leave in chylomicrons, so less fat absorption means less of them absorbed.

variables.name: Glucose absorption from the meal's starch
variables.why: Starch is digested by amylase and brush border enzymes and absorbed through SGLT1, none of which need lipase.

why.correct: SGLT1 uses the energy of sodium moving down its gradient into the cell. The pumps keep sodium inside the cell low. Once they stop, sodium inside rises, the gradient collapses, and SGLT1 can no longer pull glucose in against its own gradient.
options: Correct. With the pumps stopped, sodium leaks in and is not removed, the gradient collapses, and SGLT1 loses its energy source.
SGLT1 uses no ATP directly, but it depends on the sodium gradient that the ATP-using pumps maintain.
Sodium building up inside the cell shrinks the gradient, which slows SGLT1 rather than speeding it.
Facilitated diffusion moves glucose only down its own gradient, so it cannot keep absorption going at the same rate once lumen glucose falls.

why.correct: The toxin drives secretion but leaves SGLT1 working. Each glucose that enters through SGLT1 brings two sodium ions with it. The absorbed sodium and glucose raise the solute on the blood side, and water follows by osmosis, rehydrating the child even while secretion goes on.
options: Glucose does not kill bacteria; it feeds most of them.
The chloride secretion continues. The solution works by adding absorption, not by blocking secretion.
Correct. Sodium-glucose cotransport is the basis of oral rehydration.
The colon's epithelial cells burn mainly butyrate from bacteria, and fuel is not what limits absorption here.

why.correct: 1,400 mL reaches the colon (1,200 from the small intestine plus 200 of its own mucous secretions). It absorbs 1,250 mL. 1,250 ÷ 1,400 = 0.89, about 89%, leaving 150 mL in the feces.
options: 14% is the share of the whole day's fluid that the colon absorbs (1,250 of about 9,200 mL), not the share of what reaches it.
Correct. The colon absorbs most of what it receives.
Half would leave about 700 mL in the feces; the figure shows 150 mL.
About 98% is the share absorbed by the whole gut, small intestine and colon together.

why.correct: Absorbed long-chain fats leave the cell packaged as chylomicrons, large particles that cannot cross the wall of the villus blood capillaries. The lacteal's cells have wide gaps between them that let chylomicrons in.
options: Bile salts stay in the lumen and are reabsorbed in the ileum. The fats leave the absorptive cell as chylomicrons, without bile salts.
Lymph flows much more slowly than blood.
The villus capillaries are fenestrated and take up sugars, amino acids and short-chain fatty acids; their pores are simply too small for chylomicrons.
Correct. Size decides the route.

why.correct: Without bile salts, fat is poorly emulsified and no micelles form, so long-chain fatty acids, cholesterol and the vitamins that dissolve in fat, such as D and K, are poorly absorbed. Glucose and amino acids are water-soluble and absorbed by carriers that do not need bile.
options: Correct. Long-chain fatty acids need micelles to reach the brush border.
Correct. Vitamin K travels with fat in micelles; its loss is why obstructive jaundice can cause bleeding.
Glucose is absorbed through SGLT1, which does not need bile.
Correct. Cholesterol is absorbed from micelles.
Amino acids use carriers powered by sodium, not micelles.
Correct. Vitamin D dissolves in fat and is absorbed with it.

why.correct: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed only in the terminal ileum, by receptor-mediated endocytosis. Removing it stops B12 absorption. The liver's store lasts three to five years, so the deficiency appears years after surgery.
options: Correct. The terminal ileum is the only site where B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed.
His stomach is healthy, so parietal cells still make intrinsic factor.
His pancreas is not affected by removing the ileum.
Lactase splits lactose; it has no role in B12 absorption.

why.correct: Haptocorrin holds B12 through the stomach. In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases such as trypsin digest haptocorrin, freeing B12 to bind intrinsic factor. That is why pancreatic failure can reduce B12 absorption.
options: Correct. Pancreatic proteases hand B12 over to intrinsic factor.
B12 is water-soluble and is not carried in micelles.
Lactase splits lactose; it does not act on proteins.
B12 is absorbed by endocytosis in the ileum and leaves the cell into the blood, not in chylomicrons.

why.correct: Milk contains a lot of lactose; hard cheese contains very little. Undigested lactose holds water in the gut and is fermented by colon bacteria, causing gas, bloating and osmotic diarrhea a couple of hours later. This is lactose intolerance, not an immune reaction.
options: A milk allergy is an immune reaction to milk proteins, usually with hives, vomiting or wheezing, and cheese contains the same proteins.
Correct. Her symptoms follow the lactose content of the food.
A lipase deficiency would cause fatty stools after any fatty food, including cheese.
More lactase would digest lactose completely, and glucose is absorbed in the small intestine.

why.correct: Chylomicrons are too large for the villus blood capillaries. They enter the lacteals and travel in lymph through the thoracic duct into the veins where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet, bypassing the liver at first.
options: This step is right. Micelles carry the digested lipids through the water next to the brush border.
This step is right. The lipids cross the apical membrane; the bile salts stay in the lumen.
This step is right. Rebuilding keeps free fatty acids inside the cell low.
This step is right. Chylomicrons are triglyceride and cholesterol wrapped in phospholipid and protein.
This is the error. Chylomicrons enter the lacteals, not the blood capillaries.

why.correct: Pancreatic nucleases cut DNA and RNA into nucleotides, and brush border nucleosidases and phosphatases split the nucleotides into their parts: a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and phosphate. These are absorbed by active transport.
options: Nucleotides are split further at the brush border before absorption.
Amino acids and glucose come from proteins and carbohydrates, not nucleic acids.
Pancreatic nucleases cut RNA chains down to nucleotides.
Correct. Nucleotides are split into their three parts.

why.correct: Dipeptides and tripeptides enter on their own carrier, powered by hydrogen ions, and are split inside the cell. Neutral amino acids locked inside those short peptides still get in, so the defective single-amino-acid carrier is partly bypassed.
options: Amino acids are charged or polar and need carriers to cross the membrane.
Correct. Peptide absorption provides a second route in.
Very little amino acid absorption happens in the colon.
Pepsin cuts peptide bonds; it does not turn one amino acid into another.

why.correct: Pancreatic amylase works in the lumen and still cuts starch into maltose, maltotriose and α-dextrins. The last step, by maltase and α-dextrinase, happens on the brush border, which is damaged. So the partly digested pieces build up, unabsorbed.
options: Pancreatic amylase works in the lumen, not on the brush border, so starch is still cut into pieces.
Glucose is released by maltase and α-dextrinase on the brush border, which is damaged, so little is made.
Correct. The brush border step fails, so its substrates accumulate.
Starch is made only of glucose; galactose comes from lactose.

why.correct: Carboxypeptidase arrives in pancreatic juice as an inactive precursor, is activated by trypsin, and removes amino acids one at a time from the end of a chain that has a free carboxyl group. Its partner at the other end is aminopeptidase, on the brush border.
options: Correct. Pancreatic source, carboxyl end.
That describes aminopeptidase, which works from the amino end.
Pepsin is the stomach's protein-digesting enzyme. Carboxypeptidase works in the near-neutral small intestine.
"Carboxy" refers to the carboxyl end of a protein chain, not to carbohydrate; carboxypeptidase digests peptides.

why.correct: Vitamin K dissolves in fat and is absorbed only with micelles, which need bile salts. Without it, the liver still makes factors II, VII, IX and X, but in a form that cannot bind calcium and does not work. Giving vitamin K by injection bypasses the gut and corrects the bleeding.
options: Bilirubin causes the yellow color; it does not destroy platelets.
Correct. Fat malabsorption causes vitamin K deficiency.
There is no reason to think the tumor releases heparin.
Healthy hepatocytes keep making fibrinogen; the missing piece is vitamin K for the other factors.

why.correct: Facilitated diffusion only moves a substance down its concentration gradient. Fructose enters while the lumen holds more than the cell, so a large dose of fructose on its own can outrun the carriers, and the unabsorbed fructose causes osmotic symptoms.
options: Correct. Without a sodium partner, fructose can only move downhill.
Facilitated diffusion uses no ATP.
Fructose leaves the cell into the villus capillaries, like glucose.
Fructose's carrier does not use sodium, so it does not depend on sodium in the lumen.

why.correct: Short- and medium-chain fatty acids are soluble enough in water to cross the cell without being rebuilt into triglycerides and packaged. They enter the villus capillaries and reach the liver in the hepatic portal vein, while long-chain fats go into chylomicrons and the lymph.
options: They are absorbed, and more easily than long-chain fatty acids.
They are absorbed in the small intestine, and they are not put into chylomicrons.
Correct. Their water solubility lets them take the blood route.
Intrinsic factor is for vitamin B12 only.
